doc.title: Peter Vacher interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clearwater Beach, Florida, March 18, 2001

title: Keith Ingham and whether British jazz matches American
summary: Vacher answers Keith Ingham's remark that England has nothing as good as American jazz, citing Joe Temperley and English players who moved to New York.

story.theme_name: Going abroad: American jazz musicians touring and living in Europe
story.community_name: Going abroad: touring Europe and Japan

blocks.x: I want to tell you about Keith Ingham, who you are aware of, of course. I asked him about American musicians going to England and embracing English music, like he came over here, and he said, “Well we don’t have anything as good as American jazz.” What’s your reaction to that statement?

I think there’s a whole built-in thing which seems to imply that because America is the home of the music that Americans must be its best practitioners. And I grew up with that. But I think a little bit of perspective starts to say that today jazz is an international music. It’s a music of all nations. And I think I’d be prepared to say that we have some very fine players. Whether they have something that is so special that others this side of the pond might learn from it well I’ll leave others to say. But we have produced some fine players if you think of someone like Joe Temperley, presently with the Lincoln Center Jazz Orchestra. I don’t think we need to make any apologies for his playing capability. So maybe Keith was being a little bit — how can I put it — biased if you like. That’s not to say that I wouldn’t agree that of course the major innovators, the most considerable contributors, with the possible exception of Django Reinhardt, have been from this side of the pond.
Yeah, and I’m not sure he was just talking about the musicians either. But he thought that jazz in itself was, I guess, better for him than any kind of music that he would have found in England.
I think Keith fell in love with the music, didn’t he? © Fillius Jazz Archive -2-

And that’s what he wanted to do. And he found I think the London scene, to a degree, restricting. And like a number of other English players, George Shearing of course, Derek Smith would be others, Marian McPartland you mentioned, he saw the bigger opportunity this side of the Atlantic, New York in particular being the focal point as he saw it, I’m sure that was justified. And I know because I spoke to him in the last year that he feels that it was a wholly good move. And who’s to say he was wrong? As he sees it that must have been right for him.
